The government of [[Harris County, Texas]] maintains its main jail complex in [[Downtown Houston|Downtown]] [[Houston]], [[Texas]]. The complex, operated by the [[Harris County Sheriff's Office (Texas)|Harris County Sheriff's Office]] (HCSO), lies in the [[peninsula]] formed by the [[Buffalo Bayou]] in Northern Downtown. While most of the complex is based on county jails serving Harris County, [[Joe Kegans State Jail]] is also located within the complex. The Harris County District Court is located just next to the jail complex.

==History==
{{expand section|date=July 2019}}

===1880 Jail===
The Harris County Commissioners' Court hired [[Eugene T. Heiner]] to serve as chief architect for a new county jail to be located at the corner of Caroline Street and Preston Avenue. The previous jail had been located within the Harris County Courthouse, located at Courthouse Square, bounded by Fannin and San Jacinto streets, and by Congress and Preston avenues. This larger, free-standing jail was located two blocks away from the courthouse. The bottom two floors were decorated with arched-moldings over the windows and quoins at the corners. The third floor was formed with a mansard roof, featuring ocular windows. This jail opened in 1880.<ref>Bradley (2020), p. 53.</ref>

===21st Century===
In 2007 there was a proposal to construct a jail facility with a bond worth $245 million, but voters rejected it.<ref>{{cite news|author=Murphy, Bill|url=https://www.chron.com/news/houston-texas/article/Harris-County-jail-bond-defeated-5-others-win-1846285.php|title=Harris County jail bond defeated; 5 others win approval|newspaper=[[Houston Chronicle]]|date=2007-11-07|access-date=2018-09-11|archive-date=2018-09-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180911112826/https://www.chron.com/news/houston-texas/article/Harris-County-jail-bond-defeated-5-others-win-1846285.php|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2021 prisoners reported problems with the plumbing system and lack of heat during the [[2021 Texas power crisis]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Shepherd|first=Katie|url=https://www.chron.com/news/article/Texas-inmates-stuck-with-clogged-toilets-15962538.php|title=Texas inmates stuck with clogged toilets, freezing cells, advocates say: 'So cold that their bodies are numb'|newspaper=[[Houston Chronicle]]|date=2021-02-19|accessdate=2021-02-26|archive-date=2021-02-21|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210221234204/https://www.chron.com/news/article/Texas-inmates-stuck-with-clogged-toilets-15962538.php|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2022 the jails had higher assault rates compared to other large jails in the state.<ref>{{cite web|last=Flahive|first=Paul|url=https://www.houstonpublicmedia.org/articles/news/criminal-justice/2022/01/25/417633/advocates-and-jailers-fear-riot-conditions-as-violence-persists-in-harris-county/|title=Advocates and jailers fear riot conditions as violence persists in Harris County|publisher=[[KUHT|Houston Public Media]]|date=2022-01-25|accessdate=2022-01-26|archive-date=2022-01-25|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220125174614/https://www.houstonpublicmedia.org/articles/news/criminal-justice/2022/01/25/417633/advocates-and-jailers-fear-riot-conditions-as-violence-persists-in-harris-county/|url-status=live}}</ref> By then the rate of prisoner deaths also increased.<ref>{{cite web|last=Gundu|first=Krish|last2=Reinhart|first2=Eric|url=https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2022/10/in-custody-deaths-surging-houston-harris-county-jail.html|title=Why Are In-Custody Deaths Surging at Houston’s Harris County Jail?|work=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]|date=2022-10-25|accessdate=2022-10-28}}</ref> Lucio Vasquez of [[KUHT|Houston Public Media]] stated that Texas Senate Bill 6, which ended many forms of cashless [[bail]], may be contributing to overcrowding and deaths.<ref>{{cite web|last=Vasquez|first=Lucio|url=https://www.houstonpublicmedia.org/articles/news/criminal-justice/2022/11/03/436118/senate-bill-6-may-be-contributing-to-a-record-number-of-deaths-at-harris-county-jail/|title=Senate Bill 6 may be contributing to a record number of deaths at Harris County Jail|publisher=[[KUHT|Houston Public Media]]|date=2022-11-03|accessdate=2022-11-05}}</ref> As of October 2022, over 10,000 inmates are in the jail complex.<ref>{{cite web|last=González Kelly|first=Sam|url=https://www.houstonchronicle.com/news/houston-texas/crime/article/Harris-County-jail-deaths-17486331.php|title=2 die at Harris County jail as critics blame unsafe conditions for highest death toll in years|newspaper=[[Houston Chronicle]]|date=2022-10-05|accessdate=2022-11-05}}</ref> As of November 2022, 24 prisoners in the jail complex died in custody in the year 2022.<ref name=DewanJailDeathSent>{{cite web|last=Dewan|first=Shaila|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/11/22/us/jails-deaths.html|title=Jail Is a Death Sentence for a Growing Number of Americans|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=2022-11-22|accessdate=2022-11-24}}</ref>

In 2022, 80%<!--Source text says "four out of five"--> of the prisoners are classified as having mental health issues, and as of November 2022, more than 12<!--Source text: "[...]24 people have died this year. More than half had a history of mental problems."--> of the deaths in custody had documented issues with mental health.<ref name=DewanJailDeathSent/>

On April 5, 2024, a [[Gaza war protests in the United States|Gaza war protest]] took place outside of the jail as at least three protesters at an earlier [[Al Quds Day]] demonstration had been arrested.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Willey |first=Jessica |date=2024-04-06 |title=Crowd gathers outside Harris County Jail after 3 reportedly arrested following Al Quds Day protest |url=https://abc13.com/protest-harris-county-jail-al-quds-palestine-3-arrested/14624941/ |access-date=2024-04-06 |website=ABC13 Houston |language=en}}</ref>

==Demographics==
{{As of|2024}}, the Harris County jail facilities together have a capacity for 9,575 inmates; at times they have held over 12,000. Due to a state-mandated staffing ratio, the HCSO had to ship inmates to other jails, including some in [[Louisiana]]; in June 2010 1,600 Harris County inmates were serving time in other jails. By January 2012 the Harris County jails had 8,573, a decrease by 31% from 2008 to 2012, and there were only 21 inmates serving time in other jail facilities, all in Texas.<ref>{{cite news|author=Morris, Mike|url=https://www.chron.com/news/houston-texas/article/Thanks-to-less-crowding-overflow-inmates-staying-2447136.php|title=Thanks to less crowding, overflow inmates staying in Harris|newspaper=[[Houston Chronicle]]|date=2012-01-06|access-date=2018-09-11|archive-date=2018-09-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180911152156/https://www.chron.com/news/houston-texas/article/Thanks-to-less-crowding-overflow-inmates-staying-2447136.php|url-status=live}}</ref>

The jail population increased since the [[Texas Legislature]] cut its community mental health services funding by $400 million in 2003. Between 2004 and 2009 the population of the Harris County jails increased from 7,648 to 11,546. From 2003 to 2011 the number of full-time psychiatrists increased from three to eleven. As of 2011 25% of prisoners require mental health services. Of them, 90% had been previously placed in the Harris County jail.<ref>Hart, Patricia Kilday. "[http://www.chron.com/news/kilday-hart/article/Mental-health-facility-The-county-jail-2271150.php Mental health facility? The county jail] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190711205638/https://www.chron.com/news/kilday-hart/article/Mental-health-facility-The-county-jail-2271150.php |date=2019-07-11 }}." ''[[Houston Chronicle]]''. Tuesday November 15, 2011. Retrieved on November 23, 2011.</ref>

==Complex and facilities==

The Harris County jail complex consists of three county jails and the [[Joe Kegans State Jail]].{{citation needed|date=July 2019}}<!--Need ref that Kegans is a part of the complex-->

===1200 Jail===
[[File:1200JailHoustonTX.JPG|thumb|The 1200 Jail, the headquarters of the [[Harris County Sheriff's Office (Texas)|Harris County Sheriff's Office]]]]
The 1200 Jail (1200 Baker Street) opened on January 23, 2003.<ref name="HCSOMed">"[http://www.hcso.hctx.net/SupportSvcs/medical/default.asp Medical] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100201235524/http://www.hcso.hctx.net/SupportSvcs/medical/default.asp |date=2010-02-01 }}." Harris County Sheriff's Office. Retrieved on May 28, 2010.</ref> The 1200 Jail has the administrative offices of the Sheriff's Department. The building has {{convert|603000|sqft|sqm}} of space, and it has a {{convert|100000|sqft|sqm}} parking garage. The facility, which has 4,156 regular beds, 124 beds for the Medical Division, and 96 beds for MHMRA, is one American football field deep and two American football fields in length. 430 sheriff's deputies and detention officers work at the facility. The facility houses an inmate classification center. Each floor has counseling rooms, MHMRA examination/interview rooms, multi-purpose rooms, a recreation area, triage rooms. The fourth floor houses women. The sixth floor houses a law library and vocational rooms. The jail offers New Choices, a substance abuse program.<ref>"[http://www.hcso.hctx.net/detention/1200.asp The 1200 Jail] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101025092220/http://www.hcso.hctx.net/detention/1200.asp |date=2010-10-25 }}." Harris County Sheriff's Office. Retrieved on May 28, 2010.</ref> The 1200 Jail includes a large medical clinic, a dental facility, an infirmary, mental health facilities, a pharmacy, an x-ray facility.<ref name="HCSOMed"/>

===701 Jail===

The 701 Jail (701 North San Jacinto Street) is one of the largest detention facilities in the United States.<ref name="701North2002">"[https://web.archive.org/web/20030222132009/http://www.co.harris.tx.us/so/ih_701.htm 701 North San Jacinto]." Harris County Sheriff's Office. Retrieved on May 28, 2010.</ref> The seven floor 701 Jail has 4,144 inmate beds. The 701 Jail, originally a five-story building to be used as a cold storage warehouse,<ref name="701jail">"[http://www.hcso.hctx.net/detention/701.asp The 701 Jail] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080517122832/http://www.hcso.hctx.net/detention/701.asp |date=2008-05-17 }}." Harris County Sheriff's Office. Retrieved on May 28, 2010.</ref> opened in the late 1920s. The Houston Terminal Warehouse and Cold Storage Facility was constantly occupied throughout its history. In 1989 the county completed the planning and design stage of its new jail. The cold storage portion was allowed to thaw, and construction on the facility began in December of that year.<ref name="701North2002"/> The facility was gutted and two floors were added.<ref name="701jail"/> The 701 Jail opened in August 1991.<ref name="701North2002"/> Harris County stated that the re-use of the warehouse saved the county about $21,000,000. About 600 sheriff's deputies and detention officers work in the facility. The county designates the 701 Jail as a "Direct Observation" facility, where staff members monitor inmates continuously for 24 hours per day, 7 days per week.<ref name="701jail"/> In 2002 the 701 Jail was the second largest American jail, with the [[Los Angeles County Men's Central Jail]] of the [[Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department]] being the largest.<ref name="Jailsystem2002">"[https://web.archive.org/web/20030212092227/http://www.co.harris.tx.us/so/detention.htm Harris County Jail System]." Harris County Sheriff's Office. February 12, 2003. Retrieved on May 28, 2010.</ref>

===1307 Jail===

The 1307 Jail (1307 Baker Street<ref name="Jailsystem2002"/>), located east of the 701 Jail, was originally built as a state jail for the [[Texas Department of Criminal Justice]].<ref name="1307Jail">"[http://www.hcso.hctx.net/detention/1307.asp The 1307 Jail] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110213060608/http://www.hcso.hctx.net/detention/1307.asp |date=2011-02-13 }}," Harris County Sheriff's Office. Retrieved on May 28, 2010.</ref> The building was at first occupied by the Harris County Community Supervision and Corrections Department. The building reopened under the Sheriff's office in 1998.<ref name="Jailsystem2002"/> As of 2010 the Harris County Sheriff's Office is leasing the facility. The 1,070 inmate beds are located in two wings. The county designates this jail as a "Semi-Direct Observation," where staff members monitor inmates in the dormitory area continuously for twenty-four hours per day, seven days per week. One lieutenant, nine sergeants, and 112 sheriff's deputies and detention officers staff the jail. The jail also has the Farm Shop, a place where stray livestock confiscated by the Sheriff are kept.<ref name="1307Jail"/>

===Joe Kegans State Jail===

The [[Joe Kegans State Jail]] is a Texas state jail that generally houses inmates from Harris County serving shorter term felonies. It is the only jail in the complex that is a state facility in contrast to a county jail.<!--Need ref that Kegans is a part of the complex-->

===Former facilities===
The {{convert|850000|sqft|sqm}} 1301 Franklin facility opened on September 13, 1982.<ref name="1301Franklin2002">"[https://web.archive.org/web/20030222131407/http://www.co.harris.tx.us/so/ih_1301.htm 1301 Franklin facility]." Harris County Sheriff's Office. February 22, 2003. Retrieved on May 28, 2010.</ref> The county built the jail due to the aftermath of the early 1980s Alberti lawsuit.<ref name="301SanJacjail">"[https://web.archive.org/web/20030222131554/http://www.co.harris.tx.us/so/ih_301.htm 301 San Jacinto]." Harris County Sheriff's Office. Retrieved on May 28, 2010.</ref> The jail, with 13 stories and a basement, had the HCSO's administrative offices. The facility opened on September 13, 1982, and had the capacity to house around 4,000 inmates.<ref name="1301Franklin2002"/> After the opening of the 1200 Jail on January 23, 2003, the former Franklin facility was no longer used as a jail.<ref name="HCSOMed"/> Currently the HCSO's Crime Scene Unit, Emergency Dispatch Center(EDC), Warrants and A.F.I.S is housed in the building.<ref>"[http://www.hcso.hctx.net/FieldOps/csu/default.asp Crime Scene Unit] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100901121711/http://www.hcso.hctx.net/FieldOps/csu/default.asp |date=2010-09-01 }}." Harris County Sheriff's Office. Retrieved on May 28, 2010.</ref>

The 301 San Jacinto facility is a former jail. Before 1982 a portion of the 3rd floor had the headquarters of the HCSO. Three floors housed inmates. The basement had the booking, kitchen, laundry, and releasing areas. The commissary operated in a room on one of the housing floors. The Alberti lawsuit forced the county to build additional jails. In 2002 400 trustees were housed in the top four floors in the building. As of the same year administrative offices, court processing/holding cells, and visitation facilities were in the basement.<ref name="301SanJacjail"/> The facility's formal capacity was 409.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.co.harris.tx.us/so/ih_2.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19980220003646/http://www.co.harris.tx.us/so/ih_2.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=1998-02-20|title=1301 Inmate Housing Bureau|publisher=[[Harris County Sheriff's Office (Texas)|Harris County Sheriff's Office]]|access-date=2019-07-12}}</ref>

===Other facilities===
The Crites Vocational Center is away from the main jail area.<ref name=Blakingerjobs>{{cite web|author=Blakinger, Keri|url=https://www.houstonchronicle.com/news/houston-texas/houston/article/Changing-times-Harris-County-jail-expands-14290603.php|title=Changing times: Harris County jail expands vocational classes to include women|work=[[Houston Chronicle]]|date=2019-08-08|access-date=2019-08-11|archive-date=2019-08-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190811205548/https://www.houstonchronicle.com/news/houston-texas/houston/article/Changing-times-Harris-County-jail-expands-14290603.php|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Programs==
In the middle of the 1970s the county government established job training courses for inmates of the county jail. The state of Texas provided funding. [[Houston Community College]] (HCC) assisted with the program.<ref name=Blakingerjobs/> Vocational programs happen around Downtown and have done so since September 2004, when the former [[Atascocita]] boot camp, which once housed the programs, was closed.<ref name=Blakingerjobs/><ref>{{cite web|author=Tilghman, Andrew|url=https://www.chron.com/news/houston-texas/article/Harris-County-turns-away-from-boot-camps-1478743.php|title=Harris County turns away from boot camps|work=[[Houston Chronicle]]|date=2004-08-29|access-date=2019-08-11|archive-date=2019-08-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190811205553/https://www.chron.com/news/houston-texas/article/Harris-County-turns-away-from-boot-camps-1478743.php|url-status=live}}</ref>

The jail no longer has animal husbandry programs as generally prisoners no longer are positioned for agricultural careers. The jail officers discontinued wearing cowboy boots, television and radio repair was deemed obsolete, and the county authorities began purchasing furniture instead of reupholstering existing pieces; these actions resulted in the end of leathercraft, radio and television repair, and upholstery programs.<ref name=Blakingerjobs/>

Previously the jail only had job training for male inmates in certain programs but by 2019 began admitting female inmates into these programs.<ref name=Blakingerjobs/>

In previous eras prisoners who still had the right to vote, as in prisoners who were not convicted of felony offenses, received mail-in ballots so they could vote elections. In 2021 the jail set up a dedicated center for voting. In November of that year 96 prisoners voted.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Scherer|first1=Jasper|last2=Barned-Smith|first2=St. John|url=https://www.houstonchronicle.com/politics/houston/article/For-the-first-time-in-Texas-inmates-now-have-a-16588331.php|title=For the first time in Texas, inmates now have a polling place of their own at Harris County Jail|newspaper=[[Houston Chronicle]]|date=2021-11-03|accessdate=2021-11-23|archive-date=2021-11-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211124010948/https://www.houstonchronicle.com/politics/houston/article/For-the-first-time-in-Texas-inmates-now-have-a-16588331.php|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Overcrowding ==
The Harris County Jail has faced chronic overcrowding in recent decades. In March 1992, the jail was 43% over capacity less than a year after the opening of a new 4,000-bed facility. Police overtime arrests and drug case sentencing practices were highlighted as significant contributors to the population increase.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Mason |first=Julie |last2=Greene |first2=Andrea D. |date=March 4, 1992 |title=43% above capacity, county jail is in a bind |work=[[Houston Chronicle]] |page=1}}</ref>

A Criminal Justice Coordinating Council was created in 2009 with goals including the reduction of the jail population. A report from the same year recommended more diversion programs and revised bail bond practices.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Collier |first=Kiah |date=February 11, 2014 |title=Bid to boost size of county jail rejected State says local leaders have made 'great strides' in reducing inmate population, but it's not enough |work=[[Houston Chronicle]] |page=1}}</ref>

=== Outsourcing ===
Harris County spends $50 million of taxpayer funds annually on the outsourcing of people held in the jail.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hurtado |first=Danielle |date=2024-02-01 |title=Harris County Jail still out of compliance with state rules after quarterly meeting in Austin |url=https://abc13.com/harris-county-jail-issues-texas-commission-on-standards-meeting-compliance-status-50-million-taxpayer-money-to/14379138/ |access-date=2024-09-26 |website=ABC13 Houston |language=en}}</ref> In September 2024, Harris County announced that it would begin outsourcing people in its custody to Natchitoches Parish Detention Center, located more than 200 miles away in Louisiana. This became the County's third out-of-state outsourcing contract, in addition to ones with [[Tallahatchie County Correctional Facility]] in Mississippi and the LaSalle Correctional Center in Louisiana.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Vasquez |first=Lucio |date=2024-09-20 |title=Hundreds more Harris County inmates will be moved to Louisiana after closure of west Texas private jail |url=https://www.houstonpublicmedia.org/articles/news/criminal-justice/2024/09/20/500509/hundreds-more-harris-county-inmates-will-be-moved-to-louisiana-after-closure-of-west-texas-private-jail/ |access-date=2024-09-26 |website=Houston Public Media |language=en-US}}</ref> Tallahatchie County Correctional Facility is operated by [[CoreCivic]].

Harris County spends millions to house inmates in private, out-of-state prisons, raising concerns about oversight and accountability. Facilities like LaSalle and CoreCivic's Tallahatchie have faced allegations of neglect, abuse, and substandard care. The prisons are accredited by the American Correctional Association, whose process has been criticized as ineffective and biased. Advocates call for reducing the jail population by dismissing low-level nonviolent cases, but the district attorney has resisted.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lucio |first=Vasquez |date=March 18, 2024 |title=Harris County is ‘surrendering control’ by sending inmates out of Texas to private prisons with questionable oversight |url=https://www.houstonpublicmedia.org/articles/news/criminal-justice/2024/03/18/479621/harris-county-is-sending-hundreds-of-inmates-to-private-prisons-with-seemingly-little-oversight/?amp=1 |website=Houston Public Media}}</ref>

== Abuse and neglect of detainees ==
Harris County Jail has been known publicly as one of the most violent and deadly jails in the country. Harris County Jail has a long history of guards assaulting prisoners brutally to death, failure in protecting prisoners from assaults, solitary confinement as punishment, allowing suicides attempts of vulnerable detainees, and medically neglecting pregnant women.

Mikayla Savage, a 23-year-old woman had a miscarriage after a detention officer and other prisoners had allegedly assaulted her while in the Harris County Jail.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Vasquez |first=Lucio |date=2024-02-27 |title=A woman had a miscarriage after detention officers allegedly assaulted her in the Harris County Jail, lawsuit says |url=https://www.houstonpublicmedia.org/articles/news/criminal-justice/2024/02/27/478911/a-woman-had-a-miscarriage-after-detention-officers-allegedly-assaulted-her-in-the-harris-county-jail-lawsuit-says/ |access-date=2024-09-27 |website=Houston Public Media |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Detainee deaths ==
Between 2019 and 2024, more than 90 people have died while in the jail's custody.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Vasquez |first=Lucio |date=2024-09-19 |title=‘The guards wouldn’t do anything:’ Houston families outraged over death of loved ones in jail |url=https://www.wbur.org/hereandnow/2024/09/19/houston-jail-deaths |access-date=2024-09-26 |website=www.wbur.org |language=en}}</ref>

On February 15, 2023, the [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]] opened a federal civil rights investigation into the jail after dozens of inmate deaths in the past few years: 21 in 2021, 28 in 2022, and 4 in the first two months of 2023. The investigation looked into the February 2021 death of Jaquaree Simmons, and the January 2023 death of Jacoby Pillow. An earlier internal investigation into Simmons's death by the [[Harris County Sheriff's Office]] led to 11 firings, 6 suspensions, and one corrections worker charged for [[Manslaughter (United States law)|manslaughter]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Heyward |first=Giulia |date=February 15, 2023 |title=Dozens of inmates have died in a Houston jail since 2021. Now the FBI is investigating |url=https://www.npr.org/2023/02/15/1157215405/fbi-jail-deaths-harris-county-houston-civil-rights-investigations |access-date=February 16, 2023 |work=[[NPR]]}}</ref>
